title: Baldur, the Bright and the Mourned
summary: A lunar month with Baldr, the shining son of Odin and Frigg whose death is the great grief of the Norse myths: his story told closely, the honest debate about Christian influence, the truth about mistletoe, and a practice of kindness, peacemaking and light kept through loss.
welcome:
This journey spends about a month with Baldr (also spelled Balder or Baldur). You will read his death story closely and the poems behind it, look honestly at how little we know of his worship and at the long debate over whether his myth was shaped by Christianity, learn how people honour him today in Heathenry and on the Wheel of the Year, set up a bright shrine, keep nine nights of light and kindness, and decide at the end whether to dedicate yourself to him.

It is a self-dedication, not an initiation, and it does not replace the rites of any Heathen group or Wiccan coven. Baldr is a god of light and goodness, and also of grief: his story is about losing the best thing in the world. If you come to him in mourning, you are in the right place, but lean on the living too, and reach out to a counsellor if grief becomes too heavy.
about: Baldr is the son of Odin and Frigg, husband of Nanna and father of Forseti. Snorri says he is the best of the gods, so fair and bright that light shines from him, the wisest, mildest and most eloquent of them, and that the whitest of flowers is called “Baldr’s brow.” His hall is Breiðablik, where nothing unclean may enter. His fame rests on his death. Troubled by dreams, he was protected by an oath Frigg took from every thing in the world except the young mistletoe; Loki put a mistletoe dart in the hands of his blind brother Höðr, and Baldr fell. He was burned on his ship Hringhorni with his wife and horse, Odin laid the ring Draupnir on his pyre, and his brother Hermóðr rode to Hel to ransom him, but one giantess would not weep, and he stayed. After Ragnarök, Völuspá says, he comes back to a green new world. Evidence for any cult of Baldr is very slight: a few possible place names, a carved hall described by a skald, and a Danish version of his story in Saxo Grammaticus in which he is a warrior, not a victim. Scholars have argued for more than a century over whether the myth was shaped by Christian stories of Christ. Modern Heathens honour him with light, white flowers, mead and acts of kindness, and many modern Pagans remember him at midsummer as the sun begins to wane, a link that comes from the folklorist James Frazer rather than the old sources.
notes: Mistletoe is toxic to people and to pets in its berries, leaves and stems. Never eat it or make it into tea. If you use it on a shrine, hang it high out of reach of children and animals, and wash your hands after handling it. A picture or a carving is a perfectly good substitute.
Little evidence survives for any ancient cult of Baldr. Most devotional practice today is modern, and this journey says which is which.
Chamomile and mayweed, the plants called Baldr’s brow, can trigger allergies in people sensitive to the daisy family, and chamomile is mildly toxic to cats and dogs.

The link between Baldr and midsummer, and the idea of Baldr as a dying-and-rising sun god, come largely from James Frazer’s The Golden Bough (1913). They are used here as modern practice, not ancient fact.
Some modern writers present Baldr as a “Norse Christ.” This journey takes the debate seriously but treats Baldr as himself, a Norse god with his own story.

This app is inclusive. Baldr’s light is for everyone, of any ancestry, gender or orientation. Folkish groups that make the gods a matter of race, or use Baldr as an emblem of racial purity, are not the tradition taught here.

stages.title: Breiðablik
stages.intro: In Baldr’s hall, Grímnismál says, there is the least of evil. These first days are about making a bright, clean place for him and greeting him with light and something white.

practices.title: Set up a bright shrine
practices.instructions:
Choose the sunniest place you have: a south- or east-facing windowsill, a shelf that catches the morning. Lay down a clean white or pale yellow cloth. Add one white or gold candle in a holder, a cup or horn and a small dish.

For images: a small ring for Draupnir, a toy boat or ship picture for Hringhorni, a horse figure, sunstone, citrine, amber or clear quartz. White flowers are his: daisies, chamomile, mayweed, white roses, anything clean and bright. A picture or carving of mistletoe is a good sign of his story; if you use a real sprig, hang it high and out of reach.

Keep it spotless. Breiðablik is a place where nothing unclean may enter, so dust it and change the water often.
practices.prompt: What on your shrine catches the light?

practices.title: One quiet kindness
practices.instructions: For three days, do one kind, unglamorous thing for someone and tell no one: wash a colleague’s mug, send a thank-you, give up your seat. In the evening, tell Baldr what you did.
practices.prompt: What kindness did you do, and how did it feel to keep it quiet?

rite.title: Greeting the Bright One
rite.summary: A short first greeting in the morning light: hallow the space, offer mead, bread and a white flower, tell Baldr why you have come, and sit in the sun.

ingredients.name: A cup of mead, white wine or apple juice
A slice of white or light bread, or a small honey cake
A white flower, or a few chamomile or daisy heads
A white or gold candle in a safe holder

rite.preparation: Hold this in the morning, in daylight if you can. Wash your hands and face. Tidy the shrine and open the curtains. Set out the drink, bread and flower.

steps.title: Hallow the space
steps.instructions: Light the candle. Walk once sunwise around the room and name it holy.
steps.spoken: I hallow this place in light. Let nothing unclean enter here, and no unkind word.

steps.title: Greet him
steps.instructions: Stand in the light before the shrine and lift the cup.
steps.spoken: Baldr, son of Odin and Frigg, husband of Nanna, father of Forseti. Bright one, from whom the light shines; wisest and mildest of the gods, lord of Breiðablik. I bring you mead and bread and a white flower. Hear me.

steps.title: Say why you have come
steps.instructions: Tell him plainly why you are here: love of the light, a wish for peace, a grief you carry, a need for gentleness. Speak for a few minutes.

steps.title: Share and give
steps.instructions: Drink a sip and eat a bite of bread. Lay the flower on the shrine and put a piece of bread in the bowl.
steps.spoken: I share with you. Gift for gift. Hail Baldr!

steps.title: Sit in the light
steps.instructions: Sit in the sun, or by the brightest window, and let it fall on your face. Breathe slowly.

steps.title: Close
steps.instructions: Thank him. Snuff the candle. Later, pour the rest of the drink and lay the bread on the earth outside, in a sunny spot. Leave the flower on the shrine until it fades.
steps.spoken: Thank you, Baldr. I will come back.

rite.closing: Write down what you said and how the light felt.
rite.safety: Never leave a candle burning unattended, and keep it away from flowers and cloth, and from curtains at a sunny window. Pour drink outside or down a drain, not into houseplants. Keep offerings and flowers away from pets; chamomile is mildly toxic to cats and dogs.

stages.title: The Mistletoe Dart
stages.intro: Twelve days of reading: who Baldr is, the story of his death in all its detail, and the honest truth about how little we know of his worship and what the scholars have argued.

lessons.title: The Best of the Gods
lessons.summary: Baldr as Snorri and the poems describe him: his beauty, wisdom, family, hall, treasures and the white flower named after him.

sections.heading: So bright that light shines from him
sections.body:
Snorri Sturluson, writing in the 1220s, gives Baldr the warmest introduction of any god. In Rasmus Anderson’s 1880 translation: “Odin’s second son is Balder, and of him good things are to be told. He is the best, and all praise him. He is so fair of face and so bright that rays of light issue from him; and there is a plant so white that it is likened unto Balder’s brow, and it is the whitest of all plants.”

He goes on: “He is the wisest, mildest and most eloquent of all the asas; and such is his nature that none can alter the judgment he has pronounced.” That last line is a puzzle. The Old Norse can also be read to mean that none of his judgments can be carried out: a god of perfect judgment whose decisions somehow never take effect. Scholars disagree about which Snorri meant. Both say something about a goodness too fine for the world as it is.

sections.heading: Breiðablik
sections.body:
His hall is Breiðablik, “broad-shining.” Grímnismál lists it among the homes of the gods: “The seventh is Breithablik; Baldr has there / For himself a dwelling set, / In the land I know that lies so fair, / And from evil fate is free.” (Henry Adams Bellows’ 1923 translation, stanza 12.) Snorri adds that nothing unclean may enter there.

His wife is Nanna, daughter of Nepr, who dies of grief at his funeral and goes with him to Hel. Their son is Forseti, whose hall Glitnir is the best place of judgment among gods and men; all who come to him with disputes go away reconciled. Baldr’s line, then, is a line of judgment and peace.

sections.heading: His treasures and his horse
sections.body:
Baldr has his ship Hringhorni, the greatest of all ships, which becomes his funeral pyre. His horse is burned with him. The ring Draupnir, “dripper,” made by dwarves for Odin, which drops eight rings of equal weight every ninth night, is laid on Baldr’s pyre and sent back from Hel as a keepsake.

The white plant, Baldr’s brow, was known in Iceland as baldursbrá and in Sweden as baldersbrå. It is usually scentless mayweed (Tripleurospermum), a daisy-like seaside flower, and sometimes chamomile, which looks much the same.

knowAndDont.known: Snorri’s Gylfaginning ch. 22 describes Baldr’s beauty, wisdom and the plant; Grímnismál 12 names Breiðablik; Gylfaginning gives Nanna, Forseti, Hringhorni and Draupnir. Plant names such as baldursbrá are attested in Scandinavian folk botany.
knowAndDont.unknown: The meaning of the line about his judgments is disputed. How old the plant name is, and whether it goes back to pagan times, is unknown. We have no description of Baldr outside his death story and these few lines.

lessons.inPractice: Many devotees keep a white flower on Baldr’s shrine at all times, and some grow chamomile or mayweed in a pot for him. Some honour Forseti alongside him as the god of reconciliation.
reflect: Baldr is praised for being good, not for any great deed. What would it mean to be honoured for goodness?
Where in your life is there a judgment that is right but cannot be carried out?
further: Gylfaginning ch. 22 in Rasmus B. Anderson, The Younger Edda (1880), public domain.
Grímnismál in Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1923), public domain.
John Lindow, Murder and Vengeance among the Gods: Baldr in Scandinavian Mythology (1997).

lessons.title: Dreams, the Oath and the Pyre
lessons.summary: The death of Baldr told in full from Snorri and the poems: the dreams, Frigg’s oath, the mistletoe, the funeral, Hermóðr’s ride and the giantess who would not weep.

sections.heading: Baleful dreams
sections.body:
Baldr begins to have dreams that threaten his life. The poem Baldrs draumar opens with the gods in council: “Once were the gods together met, / And the goddesses came and council held, / And the far-famed ones the truth would find, / Why baleful dreams to Baldr had come.” (Bellows, stanza 1.) Odin rides down to Hel, raises a dead seeress, and learns the worst: in Hel’s hall, “Here for Baldr the mead is brewed.” His blind son Höðr will kill him, and another son, Váli, not yet born, will avenge him.

Frigg, his mother, does what she can. Snorri says she took an oath from fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds and serpents that they would not harm Baldr. Then the gods made a game of it, throwing things at him, and nothing hurt him.

sections.heading: The one thing left out
sections.body:
Loki, disguised as an old woman, visits Frigg and asks whether every thing has sworn. In Anderson’s translation she answers: “West of Valhal there grows a little shrub that is called the mistletoe, that seemed to me too young to exact an oath from.” Loki pulls up the mistletoe and goes to the gathering, where Höðr stands apart because he is blind. Loki offers to guide his hand: “shoot at him with this wand. Hoder took the mistletoe and shot at Balder under the guidance of Loke. The dart pierced him and he fell dead to the ground. This is the greatest misfortune that has ever happened to gods and men.”

Völuspá, the great Eddic poem of the world’s fate, gives the same moment in four lines: “I saw for Baldr, the bleeding god, / The son of Othin, his destiny set: / Famous and fair in the lofty fields, / Full grown in strength the mistletoe stood.” (Bellows, stanza 32.)

sections.heading: Hringhorni
sections.body:
The gods could not take vengeance there, because the place was a sanctuary. They carried Baldr to the shore and built his pyre on Hringhorni, but the ship would not move until a giantess, Hyrrokkin, came riding a wolf with snakes for reins and launched it with one push. Nanna’s heart broke and she was laid on the pyre beside him. Thor hallowed the fire with his hammer. Odin laid Draupnir on the pyre and, the poem Vafþrúðnismál hints, whispered something in his dead son’s ear that no one else would ever know.

The skald Úlfr Uggason described this funeral around 985 in Húsdrápa, a poem about carvings on the walls of a new hall in Iceland at Hjarðarholt. Snorri used it. It is the oldest witness we have to Baldr’s story, made in the last years before Iceland became Christian.

sections.heading: The ride to Hel and the dry tears
sections.body:
Hermóðr, another of Odin’s sons, rode nine nights to Hel to ransom Baldr. He found him in the high seat, and Hel set her condition: if all things, quick and dead, would weep for Baldr, he could return. The gods sent messengers through the world, and everything wept, men and beasts, earth and stones and trees and metals, “just as you must have seen that these things weep when they come out of frost and into heat.”

Only one did not. A giantess called Þökk sat in a cave and answered: “Thok will weep / With dry tears / For Balder’s burial; / Neither in life nor in death / Gave he me gladness. / Let Hel keep what she has!” Snorri says people believed she was Loki in disguise. The gods later bound Loki for this, and Váli, one night old, killed Höðr.

sections.heading: The return
sections.body: That is not quite the end. After the fire and flood of Ragnarök, Völuspá sees a green earth rising from the sea: “Then fields unsowed bear ripened fruit, / All ills grow better, and Baldr comes back; / Baldr and Hoth dwell in Hropt’s battle-hall” (Bellows, stanza 62). The killer and the killed, brothers again, live together in the new world.

knowAndDont.known: The full story is in Snorri’s Gylfaginning ch. 49–53, using Völuspá, Baldrs draumar, Vafþrúðnismál and Úlfr Uggason’s Húsdrápa (c. 985). Völuspá 32–33 and 62 give the mistletoe and the return.
knowAndDont.unknown: How much of Snorri’s detailed narrative is older tradition and how much his own storytelling is unknown. Frigg’s oath, Loki’s disguise and the weeping of all things appear only in Snorri. Baldr’s return in Völuspá is one of the passages most often suspected of Christian influence.

lessons.inPractice: Some devotees keep a quiet vigil on the night they choose to remember Baldr’s death, often at midsummer or before Yule, and then a morning of light and flowers for his return.
reflect: Frigg did everything she could and still missed one small thing. Is there a loss you blame yourself for that was not yours to prevent?
Þökk’s dry tears are the one refusal that keeps Baldr in Hel. What do you think of her?
further: Völuspá, Baldrs draumar and Vafþrúðnismál in Bellows (1923).
Lindow, Murder and Vengeance among the Gods (1997).

lessons.title: A God With Little Cult: Saxo, Merseburg and the Christ Debate
lessons.summary: The honest state of the evidence for Baldr’s worship, the very different Danish version of his story, and the long argument over Christian influence.

sections.heading: How little we have
sections.body:
For a god so central to the myths, Baldr leaves almost no trace of worship. No source describes a temple, priest, sacrifice or festival for him in the Viking Age. A few place names in Scandinavia may contain his name, but each is debated, since baldr was also a poetic word meaning “lord” or “hero.” The fourteenth-century Friðþjófs saga describes a sacred enclosure called Baldrshagi, “Baldr’s meadow,” with a temple where no one might harm another; it is a late romance and most scholars do not treat it as evidence of real cult.

Some gold bracteates, pendants of the fifth and sixth centuries, show a figure struck by a weapon among other figures, which the German scholar Karl Hauck read as Baldr’s death. That reading is possible and widely discussed, not secure.

sections.heading: The Danish Balderus
sections.body:
Saxo Grammaticus, writing his history of the Danes around 1200, tells a quite different story. His Balderus is a demigod warrior, son of Odin, who fights a human hero, Hotherus, for the love of Nanna. Hotherus wins Nanna, defeats Balderus in battle, and finally kills him with a magic sword. Balderus’ army, dying of thirst, is saved when he strikes the ground and a spring bursts out. In Denmark a spring near Roskilde was known as Baldersbrønd, and the story was told about it.

Saxo turns gods into men as a matter of policy, so his version is not more reliable than Snorri’s. But it shows that in Denmark, Baldr’s story could be told as a heroic feud over a woman rather than as the death of innocence.

sections.heading: The Merseburg Charm
sections.body: The Second Merseburg Charm, written down in the tenth century in Old High German, is a healing spell for a horse’s sprained leg. It begins with “Phol and Wodan” riding into a wood, when the foal of “balder” sprains its foot, and goddesses including Frija and Volla sing charms over it before Wodan heals it. Some scholars read balder as the god’s name, others as the word “lord” (so “the lord’s foal,” meaning Wodan’s). If the first reading is right, it is the oldest mention of Baldr by name, and a sign he was known far south of Scandinavia.

sections.heading: Is Baldr a Christian borrowing?
sections.body:
In the 1880s the Norwegian scholar Sophus Bugge argued that Snorri’s Baldr story was largely built from medieval Christian legend: the innocent son of the All-Father, pierced and mourned by all creation, harrowing of hell, and a return in a new world. Others answered that Húsdrápa shows the funeral story in Iceland before conversion, that Saxo and the Merseburg Charm point to older traditions, and that dying gods and mourning goddesses are found long before Christianity.

Most scholars now take a middle view. There probably was an old pagan myth of Baldr’s death, and the versions written down by Christians, especially Snorri’s, were shaped by the Christian world those writers lived in. The weeping of all creation and the return after Ragnarök are the parts most often suspected. This does not make Baldr less real or less worth honouring. It means being honest that what we hold is the story as Christian Icelanders remembered it.

knowAndDont.known: Saxo’s Gesta Danorum book 3 tells the Balderus story. The Second Merseburg Charm survives in a tenth-century manuscript. Friðþjófs saga describes Baldrshagi. Bugge, Hauck and others published the arguments described here.
knowAndDont.unknown: Whether Baldr had any organised cult is unknown. Whether “balder” in the Merseburg Charm is his name is disputed. The degree of Christian influence on his myth is unresolved and probably always will be.

lessons.inPractice: Many modern Heathens say openly that devotion to Baldr is largely modern, and honour him through the story and its values, kindness, beauty, peace and grief, rather than through reconstructed cult.
reflect: Does it matter to you whether Baldr’s story was shaped by Christianity? Why or why not?
Saxo’s Baldr is a warrior in a love feud; Snorri’s is innocence slain. Which do you recognise?
further: Saxo Grammaticus, The Danish History, books 1–9, trans. Oliver Elton (1894), public domain, book 3.
Lindow, Murder and Vengeance among the Gods (1997), on the whole debate.
Rudolf Simek, A Dictionary of Northern Mythology (1993), “Baldr” and “Merseburg Charms.”

practices.title: Greet the sun
practices.instructions: Twice a week during this stage, step outside or to a window at sunrise or in the first light you see, and greet it in Baldr’s name. Say one thing you are glad of.
practices.prompt: What were you glad of this morning?

stages.title: Nine Nights of Draupnir
stages.intro: Every ninth night the ring Draupnir drops eight more like itself. In this stage you learn the truth about mistletoe and midsummer, how Baldr is honoured today, his tides and offerings, and keep nine nights of light and kindness.

lessons.title: Mistletoe, Midsummer and Frazer
lessons.summary: What mistletoe is and why it is dangerous, why it is odd in an Icelandic story, and how Baldr came to be linked with midsummer fires.

sections.heading: A poisonous plant
sections.body:
European mistletoe (Viscum album) is a half-parasitic evergreen that grows on apple, poplar, lime and, rarely, oak trees. Its white berries, leaves and stems contain toxic proteins. Eating it can cause vomiting, slowed heart rate and, in large amounts, worse. American mistletoe (Phoradendron) is also toxic. Cats, dogs and small children are most at risk.

So: never eat mistletoe or make it into tea, whatever you read online. If you keep a sprig for Baldr, hang it high, keep fallen berries swept up, and wash your hands after handling it. Many devotees prefer a carving, a drawing, or an artificial sprig. This is not squeamishness; it is respect for the plant that killed a god.

sections.heading: A plant from somewhere else
sections.body:
Mistletoe does not grow in Iceland, and is rare in Norway, growing mostly in parts of southern Scandinavia, Denmark and further south. Some scholars think this is why the story makes a weapon of it: to Icelandic tellers it was an exotic, half-mysterious plant.

Others note that Mistilteinn is also the name of a sword in a late Icelandic saga, Hrómundar saga Gripssonar, and suggest that in an older form of the story Baldr was killed by a sword called Mistletoe, later misunderstood as the plant. Saxo’s Hotherus does kill Balderus with a sword. Either way, the mistletoe in Snorri is a small thing, too young to swear, that turns out to be fatal. That is the heart of its meaning.

sections.heading: Frazer and the Golden Bough
sections.body:
In 1913 the Scottish anthropologist James George Frazer published Balder the Beautiful, the last volumes of The Golden Bough. He argued that Baldr was a personification of the oak, that mistletoe was his life hidden outside his body, and that the great fires of midsummer across Europe were once rites of burning a god or his stand-in, with the mistletoe cut at the solstice. He connected Baldr with Scandinavian midsummer bonfires, sometimes called Balder’s balefires in his sources.

Frazer’s theories are now rejected by most scholars as far too sweeping, built on scattered folklore of many periods. But they shaped modern Paganism deeply. The idea of Baldr as a sun god who dies at midsummer, as the days begin to shorten, comes largely from Frazer, and so does the custom of remembering him at Litha.

sections.heading: Midsummer and Yule today
sections.body:
Many Pagans on the Wheel of the Year remember Baldr at Litha, the summer solstice, with bonfires, white flowers and a sense of the turning year. Many Heathens do the same at Midsummer. That is a fine modern practice, as long as it is called one.

Yule is the other natural tide. The return of the light at midwinter suits a god of light who returns after the end, and some Heathens hail Baldr on the morning after the longest night. Kissing under mistletoe at Christmas is an English custom recorded from the eighteenth century; it has nothing documented to do with Baldr, though modern retellings often connect them.

knowAndDont.known: The toxicity of Viscum album and Phoradendron is well established. Mistletoe’s distribution in Scandinavia is documented. Hrómundar saga names a sword Mistilteinn. Frazer’s Balder the Beautiful (1913) made the arguments described.
knowAndDont.unknown: Whether the original weapon was a plant or a sword is unknown. Whether Scandinavian midsummer fires had anything to do with Baldr in pagan times is unknown; the name “Balder’s balefires” is poorly attested and late. The sun-god interpretation is a modern theory.

lessons.inPractice: A common modern Litha or Midsummer custom: a candle, or a bonfire only where fires are permitted and with water at hand, at sunset on the longest day, white flowers given to the fire or the water, and Baldr remembered as the light begins to wane; then a morning of light for him at Yule.
reflect: What small thing, too young or too slight to worry about, has turned out to matter enormously in your life?
How do you feel about keeping a custom that comes from a discredited theory but has become meaningful to many?
further: James George Frazer, Balder the Beautiful (The Golden Bough, part VII, 1913), public domain, read critically.
Ronald Hutton, The Stations of the Sun (1996), on midsummer fires and Christmas customs.

lessons.title: Light Kept Through Grief: Baldr Today
lessons.summary: How Heathens and Pagans honour Baldr now, his tides and offerings, his place as a god of grief, and what not to do.

sections.heading: A god of goodness, and of loss
sections.body:
Modern devotees come to Baldr for two reasons, often both at once. Some love his light: beauty, gentleness, fairness, the dignity of simply being good. Others come in grief, because his story is one of the great stories of loss, in which a mother, a father, a wife and a whole world mourn, and the dead does not come back, not yet.

Both are true to him. Many devotees say he is a gentle presence who does not need dramatic rites, and who is honoured best by kindness, peace-making and honest praise of others. And many find comfort in bringing him their dead, because he knows the road to Hel’s hall.

sections.heading: Avoiding two mistakes
sections.body:
There are two ways people go wrong with Baldr. One is to make him bland, a sweet, passive figure with nothing to say. The stories give him wisdom, eloquence and a judgment no one can change; his son is the god of reconciliation. Gentleness is not weakness.

The other is to make him a Norse Jesus. The parallels are real and worth thinking about, but Baldr is not a saviour, does not die for anyone’s sins, and is killed by accident through malice, not by choice. Let him be himself.

sections.heading: His tides
sections.body:
No festival of Baldr is recorded. Modern devotees use the year’s turning points of light. Midsummer, or Litha, is the most common: his death remembered as the sun begins to wane. Yule (Jól), and especially the first morning after the longest night, is for his light and his return. Sigrblót, the first day of summer in the Icelandic calendar in late April, as the light comes back strongly in the north, suits him too.

Some devotees choose Sunday, the sun’s day, for a short weekly offering. That is personal practice; no weekday is his in the sources.

sections.heading: What to offer, and how
sections.body:
Mead, white wine or apple juice; white or light bread, honey cakes; white and pale yellow flowers, especially daisies and chamomile; candles lit in a sunny window. Acts are some of the best offerings: comforting someone who is grieving, making peace in a quarrel, praising someone honestly, protecting someone vulnerable, being fair when it costs you.

Offer in the morning or in daylight if you can. Name him, share a sip and a bite, give his portion, and take it outside to a sunny place afterwards. The Hávamál’s rule holds: “gifts with gifts requite” (Bellows, stanza 42). And the warning: “Better no prayer than too big an offering” (stanza 146).

sections.heading: What not to do
sections.body: Don’t eat or brew mistletoe. Don’t leave real mistletoe where pets or children can reach it. Don’t throw things at people, even in play, to imitate the gods’ game. Don’t bring quarrels to his shrine. Don’t ask him to punish Loki, Höðr or anyone else; this journey has no curses, and his own return in Völuspá is with his killer at his side. And don’t use him as an emblem of purity or race; he is a god of goodness for everyone.

knowAndDont.known: Modern devotion to Baldr is documented in Heathen and Pagan writing. Hávamál 42 and 146 give the principles of gift-giving. Forseti’s role as god of reconciliation is in Gylfaginning.
knowAndDont.unknown: None of Baldr’s modern tides or offerings is recorded in the old sources. His colours, stones and flowers are modern associations, except the white flower named for him.

lessons.inPractice: A common pattern: a white flower always on the shrine; a candle in a sunny window on Sundays; a midsummer rite of remembrance and a Yule morning of light; acts of comfort and peace-making dedicated to him through the year.
reflect: Who in your life is grieving now, and what small comfort could you offer?
Where is there a quarrel you could help to mend?
further: The Troth, Our Troth, vol. 1 (2006), on Baldr, Nanna and Forseti.

practices.title: Nine nights of light
practices.instructions:
For nine evenings, at the shrine, light the candle and set out a little mead or juice. Say Baldr’s name. Tell him one kindness you did that day, or one moment of peace you made or kept, and one thing you saw that was beautiful.

If you are grieving, say also the name of someone you have lost, and ask him to greet them in Hel’s hall.

Sit for five minutes. Snuff the candle and pour the drink outside. On the ninth night, give someone a white flower, or a small ring of any kind, for Draupnir.
practices.prompt: What kindness, what peace and what beauty did today bring?

stages.title: All Things Weep
stages.intro: Everything in the world wept for Baldr except one. Take a few days to read your journal and see what has moved you this month and what has not. Pausing, stopping, honouring Baldr at midsummer without a vow, or turning to another god are all good outcomes.

practices.title: Read your record
practices.instructions: Read everything you have written since the first rite.
practices.prompt: What has this month of light and kindness changed in you?

questions: Did this feel like meeting Baldr, or like practising kindness? Both are honest, and the second is a fine thing to keep.
Are you drawn to his light, his grief, or both? Can you hold both?
How do you feel about honouring a god with almost no recorded cult, whose myth may have been shaped by Christianity?
If you came in grief, is a dedication the right step now, or would it be better to wait?
What offering and act of kindness or peace-making can you keep for a year?
If you stop here, what will you keep from this month?

stages.title: The Ring on the Pyre
stages.intro: If you have chosen to go on, this is the dedication: a morning blót of light, a vow written in advance, and a ring hallowed as a token, after Draupnir. It is a self-dedication between you and Baldr. It is not an initiation into any group or coven, and it does not replace a group’s own rites. Make the vow gentle and true.

practices.title: Write the vow
practices.instructions: A day before, write your vow: the offering you will keep (for example, a white flower and a candle each Sunday), the act you will keep (for example, one quiet kindness each week, or one act of peace-making each month), how long (a year and a day is common), and what you ask (gentleness, light in grief, the wisdom to judge fairly).

rite.title: Dedication to Baldr
rite.summary: A morning blót in the light: hallow the space, hail Baldr, share mead and bread, swear your vow, hallow a ring as your token, and give him his share.

ingredients.name: A horn or cup of mead, white wine or apple juice
A small loaf of white bread or a honey cake
White flowers, such as daisies, chamomile or white roses
A white or gold candle in a safe holder
A token: a small plain ring, or a sunstone or amber bead

rite.preparation: Hold this in the morning, in daylight. Clean the shrine until it shines. Open the curtains. Set out the drink, bread, flowers and ring. Midsummer morning, the morning after Yule’s longest night, or the morning after your ninth night are good times.

steps.title: Hallow in light
steps.instructions: Light the candle. Walk once sunwise around the room and name it holy.
steps.spoken: I hallow this place in light. As in Breiðablik, let nothing unclean enter here.

steps.title: Hail him
steps.instructions: Stand in the light and raise the horn.
steps.spoken: Baldr, son of Odin and Frigg, beloved of Nanna, father of Forseti. Bright one, best of the gods, wisest and mildest and most eloquent. You for whom all things wept, who wait in Hel’s hall and will come back to the green new world. I come to give myself to your light. Hear me.

steps.title: Share and give
steps.instructions: Break the bread. Put the first piece in the bowl. Eat a piece and drink a sip. Lay the flowers on the shrine.
steps.spoken: I share with you. These flowers are white as your brow. Hail Baldr!

steps.title: Swear the vow
steps.instructions: Stand in the light. Read your vow aloud, once, clearly.
steps.spoken: Before Baldr, in the light of morning, I make this vow. Let it hold as long as I keep it.

steps.title: Hallow the ring
steps.instructions: Hold the ring up to the light, then pass it over the candle at a safe height. Wear it or keep it on the shrine.
steps.spoken: As Draupnir went with Baldr to the pyre and came back from Hel, let this ring be a sign of my troth. When I see it, let me remember the light in the dark.

steps.title: Pour his share
steps.instructions: Pour the rest of the horn into the bowl.
steps.spoken: Gift for gift. This is yours. Give me gentleness and fair judgment, and light in grief.

steps.title: Sit in the light
steps.instructions: Sit quietly in the sun or by the window for a few minutes.

steps.title: Close
steps.instructions: Thank him. Snuff the candle. Take the bowl outside and pour it out in a sunny spot. Share the rest of the bread with someone, and do one kindness today.
steps.spoken: Hail Baldr, and thanks. The vow is made.

rite.closing: Write the date and your vow in your journal and keep the paper copy for your rededication.
rite.safety: Keep the candle away from flowers, cloth and curtains, and never leave it burning. Do not use real mistletoe in this rite; if it is on the shrine, keep it high and out of reach. Pour drink outside or down a drain, not into houseplants. Keep flowers and food offerings away from pets.

stages.title: Until Baldr Comes Back
stages.intro: Keep the offering and the kindness you vowed. Honour Baldr at Midsummer or Litha as the light begins to wane, at Yule as it returns, and at Sigrblót as summer begins. Each year, read your vow, say how you kept it, and renew it.

practices.title: The weekly flower
practices.instructions: Once a week, put a fresh white flower on the shrine, light the candle in daylight, and tell Baldr one kindness you did that week.
practices.prompt: What kindness did you do this week?

practices.title: Keep the tides of light
practices.instructions: At Midsummer or Litha, Yule and Sigrblót, hold a blót with Baldr hailed: at midsummer, remember his death at sunset; at Yule, greet his light on the first morning after the longest night.
practices.prompt: What did you offer at this tide, and what light did you see?

practices.title: Yearly rededication
practices.instructions: On midsummer morning or the anniversary of your dedication, repeat the rite. Read last year’s vow first and say how you kept it.
practices.prompt: How did last year’s vow go, and what will this year’s be?
